title: Measurement of Health System Performance and Its Contribution Towards Health Services Utilization
abstract: IntroductionA health system is a combination of all the organizations, institutions and resources whose primary purpose is to improve health. This includes direct health service provisioning as well as efforts to influence health determinants. Through a combination of public health actions and a pyramid of health care facilities delivering personal health care services, preventive, promotive, curative and rehabilitative interventions are delivered by the health system. They are central to the healthy development of individuals, families and societies everywhere. The way health systems are designed, managed and funded affects people’s lives and livelihoods. Whatever standards are applied, it is evident that health systems in some areas perform well, while others perform poorly.Major barriers shared by programmes lie in domain of effective governance, human resources management, financing and drugs and supply systems. Identifying practical, simple and understandable methods to assess health system performance, with its complex interlinked dimensions, remains a challenge. As mentioned in World Health Report 2000, questions about health system performance have no clear or simple answers, as outcomes are hard to measure. It is difficult to establish causal attribution to health system’s contribution after controlling the effect of other factors. This gets further complicated by the lack of locally adapted tools which can be used to measure health system performance at lowest healthcare delivery levels in the hierarchy.Tools available in literature have also been conspicuous for their lack of holistic coverage of all health system domains. The tools that deal with health facility assessment gather information on resource management, and to some extent service delivery at health facilities, but altogether skip other building blocks like administrative and managerial environment, functioning of health information system and efforts for financial risk management at this level. Another gap exists in terms of lack of a single summary measure that can condense all parameters and then define the performance of health system in place as a single value. Development of a single measure summarizes the whole gamut of results, spread across various dimensions (across various building blocks in present case) and presents the information on performance in an easily comprehensible manner. World health report in 2000 had attempted to develop a single summary measure, but it was criticized for its inconsistency and lack of transparent methodology.Another point of contention that this report generated was associated with the high extent of confidence it placed in the health system for affecting the health of population in the community. Though the contribution of the medical services towards improving health and better living cannot be judged less in any way, many researchers have given more credit to socio-demographic, political and economic changes for these results. The literature is full of evidence in favour of the same. Inputs and contribution of the health system towards the overall health of community is thus a matter of never ending debate, no satisfactory conclusion towards which has ever been obtained. In view of all this background, and considerations on the current scenario as discussed, this proposed research sought to find answers to various dimensions of health system performance. The present research was carried out with the following objectives in mind:1. To develop a tool to measure Health System Performance at district level.2. To compute a summary measure, ‘Health System Performance Index’, for assessment of overall performance ofhealth system at district level.3. To develop a model to assess the relationship between health system performance and primary care coverage and curative care utilization in public sector health facilities.4. To explore role of socio-demographic factors along with health system performance in determining overall health of the community.MethodologyFramework, indicators and toolsBuilding block framework proposed by World Health Organization in 2007 was used as the guiding framework for the purpose of this research work. This framework proposed practical ways to organize health systems into 6 operational “building blocks”:a. Service deliveryb. Health workforcec. Information systemd. Medical products and technologiese. Financingf. Leadership and governanceA literature review was performed to identify existing study tools and their indicators which measure the health system in totality or separate building blocks. Search terms were developed and published literature was searched.A broad range of indicators covering all the building blocks, as proposed by WHO framework, were enlisted. Care was taken to select indicators on the basis of their usefulness in planning and development process by managers at local levels, and extent to which they can be objectively measured. Inputs on availability of data in local settings, at state, district and health facility level was solicited from programme managers at state and district level in the department ofhealth in Haryana.This list was discussed with an expert panel for inputs towards finalization of indicators for the research study. Subject experts in the field of health systems, epidemiology and biostatistics, healthcare financing, governance and health promotion, clinicians, hospital administrators and health system researchers were identified to be part of the expert panel. The experts’ opinion and final consensus on indicators was obtained by use of a group interaction process. The same process was followed for generation of study tools. The six health system building blocks were further classified into twenty sub-domains. A total of 70 input and process indicators were selected to measure performance. A set of four sub-domains for outputs and three sub-domains for assessing outcomes of the health system at district level were identified. Twenty-eight indicators were selected for measurement of their performance. A total of 13 study tools were drafted and employed for collection of data on selected indictors. The pre-test of study tools was carried out in nine purposively selected public health facilities in Panchkula district of Haryana state after which suitable modifications were made.Data collectionAll 21 districts in Haryana state were covered for final data collection. In each district, primary data was collected from 18 facilities, including 15 primary (10 SCs and 5 PHCs) and 3 secondary (2 CHCs and 1 DH) level facilities selected through a stratified random sampling approach. A facility readiness survey was undertaken besides a key informant interview of facility in-charge in each health facility. Additionally, facility in-charges and information assistants (HMIS handlers) were administered MIS familiarity and conceptual understanding tests to test their knowledge and understanding of routine HMIS systems. Motivation and job satisfaction questionnaires were administered to healthcare providers at selected facilities and at district headquarters. Client interviews were conducted with 2 indoor and 3 outdoor clients at all PHCs and higher facilities selected for the study across all districts.Secondary data on selected indicators was collected from district and state health directorate headquarters, including state NHM headquarters, state Director General Health Services (DGHS) office, State Institute of Health and Family Welfare (SIHFW) and State Civil Registration Department (Births and Deaths). Additionally, data on selected indicators was analysed using data from a community based survey - Concurrent Evaluation of NHM, undertaken in all districts of Haryana from 2012-15.Data entry and analysisThe data collected was entered in data entry tools developed in Microsoft Excel. Consistency checks and range checks were employed to minimize data entry errors. Data were subjected to normality checks using suitable statistical software. Indicators were also checked for collinearities (correlation > 0.92) with other indicators within the same sub-domain.Indicators were subsequently normalized for making them comparable and suitable for aggregation. Min-max approach was used for this purpose. The usual approach of obtaining goalposts (minimum and maximum values) for normalization from range of values in dataset (relative goalposts) was followed in 26% building block indicators and 60% health system output and outcome indicators. For the rest, theoretically minimum and maximum achievable values 0% and 100% (absolute) were used as the goalposts. The aggregation of normalized indicators was done using geometric mean approach, as the indicators were ratio scale and non-comparable in nature. Individual indicators were first aggregated to generate sub-domain scores, which were then aggregated to generate building block scores. The building block scores were aggregated to generate Health System Performance Index for inputs and processes (HSPI). Same methodology was adopted to aggregate indicators under health system output and outcome domains to compute four output sub-domain scores and three outcome sub-domain scores. The output sub-domains were then aggregated together to generate Health System Output index while outcome sub-domains were aggregated together to generate Health System Outcome index. The robustness of the composite indicator results in this study was checked employing different approaches of normalization and aggregation.Non-parametric correlation coefficients (Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient) and their significance levels were computed to assess the relationships between health system performances index and different health system outputs and outcomes. Correlations were also assessed between mentioned outputs and outcomes and sub-domains of building blocks. Relationships between different sub-domains of all six building blocks were also assessed. To fulfil the last objective of the study, contribution of health system along with social determinants of health in predicting health status of population in the community was explored. Health system outcomes, mortality rates index and morbidity rates index defined earlier were employed as indicators for health status of the community. The independent precursor variables for health of the community included Health System Performance Index (representing health system building blocks) along with other social determinants of health outside the health system purview. These social determinants of health indicators were selected from domains representing individual characteristics and behaviours of people, social and economic environment, physical environment, demographic and development characteristics of the districts in which people resided. Associations between social determinant indicators and morbidity and mortality indices were computed using nonparametric (Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients) correlations. Linear regression methods were also used to assess the association of Health System Performance Index to morbidity and mortality indices after adjustment for a summary indicator for social determinants.Ethical clearanceEthical clearance for the proposed research was obtained from the Institute Ethics Committee of Post-Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, India. Administrative approvals were obtained from National Rural Health Mission, Haryana and Director General Health Services, Haryana. Written informed consent was obtained from study participants.ResultsThe health facility surveys were conducted at 377 health facilities across Haryana. These included 20 district hospitals, 42 CHCs, 105 PHCs and 210 SCs. Tools for testing familiarity with HMIS and conceptual understanding of facility in-charges and data handlers was administered to 460 respondents, while motivation and job satisfaction tools were administered to 1749 healthcare providers, ranging from ANMs at SCs to Deputy Civil Surgeons and Civil Surgeons. Client satisfaction interviews were conducted with 833 clients of the public health system.Performance of districts on individual indicatorsAverage absorptive capacity of districts to utilize funds received in financial year 2014-15 from state NHM headquarters was found to be 79.1%. Around 3.6 core healthcare workers (doctors, specialists, staff nurses, ANMs) per 10000 population were observed in the public healthcare system. More than 78% of the sanctioned positions for this workforce were observed to be occupied.Staff productivity at PHC level ranged between 3 cases to 29 cases among different districts. Monthly provider productivity at SC level across the state was 25 ANC examinations per ANM. Provider productivity at CHC level and DH level in Haryana was found to be 17 and 29 per clinical staff per month respectively. The motivation levels of outreach staff were 85% while that of clinical staff were 78%. Motivation and job satisfaction levels were relatively lower for the administrative cadres.Average functional equipment and furniture availability at SCs across the state was 76% and 78% respectively. Nearly two-thirds (64%) of the drugs surveyed were found to be available at SC level. PHCs in state were better equipped than SCs on all four aspects. Average CHC equipment and furniture readiness across the state was 52% and 71% respectively. Availability of functional equipment at district hospitals ranged from 52% to 92% in different districts. At this level, availability of furniture, drugs and support services were found to be of 95%, 88% and 95% in the state. DHs in state were better equipped than CHCs in terms of equipment, furniture and basic amenities whereas they were almost equivalent in terms of drugs. Also, PHCs were best equipped in the state, closely followed by DHs, then CHCs and finally SCs.Average HMIS resource availability at facilities in the state was found to be 93%. More than 96% of targeted workforce were found to have received training in HMIS in the state. However, familiarity with HMIS single reporting tool was found to be only 21.2% in the state. HMIS suffered both reporting and quality issues. At state level, 83.9% of expected reports were received by the state headquarters, of which 75.6% were received on time. Data availability at facilities for local decision making was found to be around 75% in the state.Average population size served by PHCs in Haryana was found to be 37882. Effective doctor presence rate at PHCs and CHCs was found to be 81.5% in the state. Only 22.9% of FRUs had functional blood banks. Less than one-fourth PHCs in the state had at least one female doctor working at the facility, however more than half PHCs were reported to be delivering 24x7 maternity services to the community. System clients provided a 71% score to quality of basic amenities at PHCs and higher facilities in the state, while they reported an average delay of 12 minutes for OPD consultation at PHCs and higher facilities.Around 78% surveyed facilities in the state had 3 or more meetings of RKS/ VHSNC committee in the last 6 months prior to survey. The district authorities were rated 87% on approachability index in the state. Citizen charter was found to have been displayed in full public view at 86.6% of surveyed facilities in the state. All surveyed facilities reported at least 1 financial audits in last 1 year. Less than 14% system employees levelled claims of facing any type of discrimination (gender/ caste/ religion) in their job. The state scored well in terms of essential administrative skills and overall quality of administration reported by employees. About 56% maternal deaths were found to be audited by the system. DHFWS meetings were also found to be irregular.In terms of health system outputs and outcomes, the state registered an institutional delivery rate of 84%, full ANC rate of 34%, full vaccination rate of 76%, contraception prevalence rate of 61% and ORS use rate of 47% for childhood diarrhoea cases. Low bed occupancy rates (35%) were observed in rural areas, while over-burden in urban areas (169%). The public health system overall, had just 0.67 OPD visits per capita in a year. Catastrophe due to OOP expenditure on hospitalizations was faced more by the poorer strata in the community (concentration index = -0.17). The rate of high risk pregnancy detection (2.7%) as well as identification and referral of sick neonates (3.25%) were lower than the expected values. A 10.6% illness rate in last 15 days and a hospitalization rate of 3.6% in last 1 year was observed in the state. The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) and Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) ranged between 13 to 54 per 1000 live births and 74 to 200 per 1000 live births respectively among various districts in the state. About 35% of pregnant women reported to have incurred OOP expenditure for availing institutional delivery at public health facilities. For 34% patients, the hospitalization expenditure proved to be catastrophic. An average of 7% population was found to be covered under any health insurance scheme.Performance of districts on composite indicatorsRelative positions of districts in 4 quartiles were generated after division of difference between highest and lowest scores obtained by districts into 4 equal parts. While only 1 district performed exceptionally well to appear in top quartile for health financing, majority performed better than state average. In the human resources domain, it was found that 3 districts were in bottom quartile with a total of 12 districts performing below state average. A good number of districts appeared to be doing well in terms of HMIS (with 11 of 21 districts appearing in top quartile), while worrisome figures were observed in service delivery and governance domains.Twelve out of 21 districts performed better than state average on equity in health financing parameter, with four districts appearing in the top quartile. Most of districts scored well in terms of efficiency and equity in service delivery as well. In terms of utilization of curative care services, most of the districts were aggregated towards the bottom of the spectrum. Coverage of primary care services was comparatively more uniform, with only one district in the bottom quartile and total eight performing below average.Correlations of building block sub-domains with health system outcomesTests for assessing relationships between Health System Performance Index (based on inputs and processes for the six building blocks) and health system outputs and outcomes yielded a variety of results. While overall ‘Health System Outputs and Outcomes’ index correlated in a strong positive manner with Health System Performance Index (Rho = 0.53, p-value = 0.01), its break-up into health system outputs and outcomes presented a different scenario. Health system outputs index was not correlated with HSPI. However, on further stratification, it was observed that non-visible outputs were not significantly correlated with HSPI (Rho = 0.1, pvalue = 0.63), while the visible outputs index was positively correlated with HSPI which was statistically significant (Rho = 0.44, p-value = 0.04).Morbidity index outcome in state was found to be strongly positively correlated with Human Resources Building Block (Rho = 0.5, p-value = 0.02) and HMIS building block. Mortality index instead presented a strongly significant positive correlation with Service Delivery building block. Mortality index and Financial Protection indices, which represent health system outcomes, also presented strong positive correlation with health system visible outputs index. Efficient and equitable service delivery output of the health system was strongly correlated with Human Resources building block (Rho = 0.46, p-value = 0.03), while weakly correlated with Material Resources and HMIS building blocks. On similar lines, Curative care utilization output had strong positive correlations with Human Resources, Material Resources and HMIS building blocks indices of the health system.Strong positive correlations were observed between morbidity index (and hence inverse with morbidity rates) and capacity and productivity of human resources and CHC facility readiness. Morbidity index also showed strong inverse correlation with participation and responsiveness characteristics of governance building block. Mortality index strongly correlated to PHC facility readiness (Rho = 0.45, p-value = 0.04) and service availability. PHC facility readiness and Service Availability sub-domains of the building blocks presented strong positive correlations with Financial Protection outcome. Curative care utilization by community was observed to be strongly linked with SC, PHC and DH facility readiness and overall Service Availability index. Higher primary coverage index was linked with better HMIS data quality, higher service availability and higher accountability in governance.Correlations among building block sub-domainsThe capacity and productivity of human resources increased with increase in feedbacks frequency and local data availability, captured in the form of data usage index. Increase in effectiveness and efficiency in Governance had a strong positive influence on motivation and job satisfaction. SC facility readiness was observed to be strongly correlated with motivation of human resources (Rho = 0.48, p-value = 0.03) while PHC facility readiness related more with capacity of human resources. Availability of resources for HMIS was strongly related to overall PHC facility readiness and weakly to CHC facility readiness in the districts. Participation and responsiveness of the public health system was found to increase in response to decline in availability & distribution of HR, capacity & productivity of HR and HMIS data usage (Rho = -0.47, -0.44 and -0.68 respectively). Accountability in the system increased with increase in effectiveness and efficiency in governance (Rho = 0.48, p-value = 0.02).Correlations of outcomes with social determinants of healthMorbidity index was observed to be significantly correlated to two other social determinants of health apart from Health System Performance Index. These were improved drinking water source (Rho = 0.46, p-value = 0.03) under household characteristics and amount of exports (Rho = -0.54, p-value = 0.01), which is an indicator of district economic activity. Mortality index, on the other hand, was correlated with a number of social determinants of health, but not with HSPI. Highest positive correlations were observed with percent urban population in the district (Rho = 0.70, p-value < 0.01), female literacy rate (Rho = 0.69, p-value < 0.01) and district wise per capita income (Rho = 0.67, p-value < 0.01).DiscussionThe study presents a novel methodology for comprehensive assessment of all domains of public health system. A composite ‘Health System Performance Index' for relative comparison of different districts on the basis of input and process indicators was developed which has never been reported from India.Findings in context of previous evidencePresent study’s results in individual domains were similar to those previously reported from India. For Human resources for health, Rao et al in 2011 reported Haryana to have between 16-22 healthcare workers per 10,000 population, out of which 30% were employed in public health sector. Sharma M et al in 2014 reported 70% job satisfaction levels among doctors at a tertiary care centre in Chandigarh, which was less than what was found in present study from the state of Haryana. Present study points to a lower job satisfaction level among clinical healthcare workforce (71.6%) than outreach workforce (79.3%). Similar results were reported by Kumar P et al in 2014 from national capital New Delhi when they stated a higher job satisfaction among ANMs than Medical Officers.Present study found higher availability of drugs and vaccines at the public health facilities than previously reported in literature. A study from neighbouring state of Rajasthan in 2012 reported only 78.4% (116) of the PHCs to be properly equipped to provide 24-hours normal delivery facility. This was similar to present study’s findings for equipment availability at PHCs. A rapid assessment report published by NRHM, Haryana in 2013 for district Jind reported 65% facility readiness for new-bom care services at public health facilities. This was close to present study results for overall facility readiness at public health facilities in the district (71%). Issues with quality of HMIS in public health system in Haryana have been earlier highlighted by Sharma A et al in 2016. Better timeliness of emergency referral transport services have been reported by Prinja S et al in Haryana state.Relationships between health system inputs, processes and outputs, outcomesSignificant correlations observed between Health System Performance Index (based on inputs and processes) and visible outputs of the health system, which comprise of curative care utilization rates and primary care coverage rates were in accordance with the expectation that since primary care coverage and curative care utilization rates are commonly reported in routine HMIS, and hence are a subject ofintense scrutiny as a measure of performance of the health system, all inputs and processes are directed towards attainment of these goals. Significant correlations between HSPI and morbidity index, along with acute illness rate and hospitalization rate, but neither with mortality index, nor its components infant mortality rate and maternal mortality ratio could be explained by the proximity of morbidities as an outcome to the health system outputs of curative care utilization and primary care coverage.In accordance with the general expectation, it was observed under the study that curative care utilizations rates were better in districts with higher SC, PHC and DH facility readiness and overall service availability. Capacity of the human resources comparatively played a weaker role in comparison to facility readiness indices. The results show that higher coverage of primary care indicators was correlated with better HMIS data quality and higher accountability indices under governance building block. These results could be interpreted in both the ways, as the districts that maintain and report better quality HMIS have higher coverage of primary care indicators, or that districts with better coverage of primary care indicators take care to maintain better quality HMIS than those districts with poorer coverage of these indicators. Previous literature however agrees that improving quality of HMIS in place can lead to improvement in health indicators as it serves to monitor the performance and quality of the health services being provided.The study results show that equity in health financing had a significant correlation with SC facility readiness, while equitable service delivery was related to PHC facility readiness and capacity of human resources employed. As sub-centres are primarily entrusted for delivery of preventive and promotive ante-natal care services in the public health system, these must prove useful in preventing wealth related inequities due to OOP expenses at the time of delivery. Relationship between equitable service delivery and PHC facility readiness can be explained to some extent by the fact that PHCs are located in rural areas and are utilized by people from lower socio-economic quintiles as compared to secondary level healthcare facilities located in cities catering to comparatively higher socio-economic quintiles of population.Increase in public health expenditure was also found to be resulting in higher availability and distribution of human resources in the public health system, though this was a weak correlation. However, it was seen that the quality of HMIS system in place improves with improvement in availability and distribution of manpower.Results of the current study revealed SC facility readiness to be significantly correlated with motivation of human resources, while PHC facility readiness was related to capacity of human resources. It was observed that the service availability sub-domain in the study results was significantly related to availability and functionality of material resources at SC, PHC and district hospitals levels. Weak associations were also observed with motivation and job satisfaction of HR. The quality of services provided were found to have an inverse relationship with the productivity of human resources, hence, districts with higher work load at facilities presented with lower quality of services as reported by the clients in their satisfaction interviews.Relationships between health system outcomes and social determinantsPresent study results indicate that apart from the relationship with performance of public health system (HSPI), morbidity index was significantly correlated to two other social determinants of health. These were improved drinking water source, which reflected household characteristics in the population and amount of exports from the districts, which was an indicator of district economic activity. In contrast, mortality index was found to correlate strongly and significantly with a number of social determinants. These correlations were observed with indicators in all categories of social determinants. Mortality appeared to be lower in districts with higher use of clean cooking fuels and improved sanitation sources, in line with the evidence from previously published studies in literature which have linked these with different facets of mortality. Female literacy rates and health awareness levels in present study were also significantly inversely correlated with mortality rates. Many previously published studies have reported similar findings. While most of the articles and reports in the literature have assessed the importance of health behaviours, social circumstances and environment, a statement on tentative contribution of medical care provided by healthcare system has been reported by some of the publications. The low attribution of overall health to medical or clinical care (or healthcare spending) in these studies is similar to the results of present study.ConclusionsSteps towards improvement of health system can be taken only if it is understood in its entirety, yet explained in a non-complex manner. The present study presents a novel approach to summarize various components of the system into a single index, utilizing concepts and recommendations proposed by pioneers like WHO and OECD. This allows to make indicators on all aspects and dimensions of the health system a part of the assessment.Nature of the indicators selected proves it is possible to identify health system bottlenecks and priority areas for health system improvements. Study results indicate that though all building blocks of the health system are important in their own aspect, it is their interdependence on each other that makes the system work. Changes in health system governance like better efficiency and transparency can have a cascading effect on motivation and job satisfaction of employees, which results in higher facility readiness, better service availability and higher quality ofservice delivery to the community at public health facilities. This should be supplemented with efforts towards increasing absorptive capacity of the districts and hence public health spending per capita, which leads to higher availability of human resources in the system and better facility readiness in terms of material resources, which leads to higher utilization of curative care services by the population. The results also bring to notice current lack of focus on equity dimensions of health financing and service delivery. This is an important area of concern and policy decisions shall also take these into account for consideration while framing policies for improving visible outputs of the health system.Results of the study also open new fronts, on which further research can be established in the future in order to gamer a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms. Qualitative research methods may be employed to better comprehend relationships of individual health system building block sub-domains with outputs & outcomes of the system. Contributions of researchers from other scientific disciplines like public administration and business management may greatly enhance performance of building blocks like governance and administration and healthcare financing. A team work of health system researchers, program managers and researchers from other domains of science and humanities is the necessity of the hour, which can provide potentially viable and efficient solutions to bring an everlasting change in the current situation.

title: Implementation and evaluation of a community walking blood bank for haemorrhagic shock when banked blood is unavailable: protocol for a mixed-methods, effectiveness-implementation study – phase 2 of the Local Initiative for emergency blood (LIFE-Blood) study
authors: Kumar Nikathan; Fleming, Mathew; Sawhney Riya; Thompson, Avery A; Makanga Cindy; Williams, Wendy; Wesonga Caroline; Musa Abdirahman; Nyanamba Nicodemus OM; Lokuruka Kristina Kuya; Barmasai Hillary; Wakwabubi Maurice; Wangia, Elizabeth; Opiyo Cavin Otieno; Epem, Esekon; Gilchrist Lokoel; Puyana, Juan Carlos; Kumar, Pratap; Delaney, Meghan; Nobhojit, Roy; Cap, Andrew P; Dey Tanujit; Omondi Onyango Stephen; Mutebi, Edward; Hongo, Kevin; Raykar Nakul; Chelagat Tecla; Barnes, Linda
abstract: IntroductionTrauma, obstetric haemorrhage and severe anaemia lead to millions of deaths every year. Many of these deaths occur in regions known as ‘blood deserts’ where there is virtually no access to blood transfusions. A community or civilian walking blood bank (CWBB) is a low-resource strategy that can provide just-in-time, point-of-care tested blood transfusions in blood deserts when banked blood is not readily available and the alternative is almost-certain death. This protocol is designed to evaluate the effectiveness and implementation of a CWBB at Lodwar County Referral Hospital located in a blood desert in rural north-west Kenya.Methods and analysisWe will use a mixed-methods approach relying on an implementation science design to evaluate effectiveness, acceptability, applicability and impact of a CWBB. The study will be conducted over 1 year in two parts: pre-emergency and post-emergency transfusion protocol (ETP) implementation. First, a previously developed ETP will be validated and finalised by key hospital stakeholders. Effectiveness will be assessed quantitatively and qualitatively. Prospective laboratory-based data collection will measure changes in blood ordering practices. We expect a sample size of approximately 140 (20/month) unmet blood transfusion requests, with 40 (5/month) of those being emergent (requiring blood in less than 2 hours). These cohorts will be compared pre-implementation and post implementation. Qualitatively, key informant interviews of hospital staff and the community will explore clinical blood demand and general understanding and perceptions about blood donation and transfusion. Lastly, we will determine the adaptability and scalability of a CWBB to other low-resource settings with in-depth interviews and a modified Delphi approach to achieve consensus regarding key components of a CWBB and its transferability to other settings.Ethics and disseminationEthical approval was granted by the Strathmore University Institutional Scientific and Ethics Review Committee (SU-ISERC2234/24) and the Mass General Brigham (MGB) Hospital’s Institutional Review Board (#2024P001878; #2024P001879; #2024P001885; #2024P001887). The study team also secured a research licence from the National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation (#168094) before initiating the study. Interviews will be voluntary and consent will be obtained prior to participation. Blood transfusion consent will be collected as per standard hospital process. The findings will be disseminated through academic publications, conference presentations and workshops, contributing valuable insights into emergency blood transfusion protocols. These findings will also be conveyed to Lodwar County Referral Hospital in order to facilitate quality improvement.

title: El abastecimiento de agua en el Madrid de Fernando VI (1746-1759): funcionarios, procedimientos y documentos

Se estudia su faceta histórico-administrativa y documental, abordando el acceso a la profesión a través de los expedientes que se han conservado en el Archivo de Villa de Madrid.
